CCAR-P · Claude Certified Architect: Professional · 63 items · 120 min · pass 720/1000

Domain 1: Solution Design & Architecture

17% of the exam, about 11 items. This domain tests whether you can turn a business problem into a working Claude system. You pick the right pattern. You shape the full pipeline. You break hard problems into pieces. You tie every technical choice to money, speed, and a measurable promise.

Items are scenario based. They reward the narrowest design that satisfies the stated constraint. They punish over-engineering.

D1 · 17% · ~11 itemsMultiple-choice + multiple-responseScenario: design decisions & trade-offsPearson VUE · $175

Unit 1: Translating business problems into Claude-based solutions

On the board.

A VP says "our support team cannot keep up with the tickets, can Claude fix it?" Three questions matter. What do you ask first? What do you measure? How do you decide the shape: a workflow, an agent, or no LLM at all? That is the whole unit in one question.

1.1 The vague ask: clarify before you measure

Rung 1: the true beginning. Real projects never start with a clean spec. They start with a sentence like "our support team cannot keep up with the tickets, can Claude fix it?" Your first job is not architecture. Your first job is to ask questions. A vague ask hides three facts you need: what hurts, who it hurts, and what limits you must respect. Ask until you can write all three down.

The answers become your constraints. The constraints do half the design work before you pick any pattern.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left (the vague ask): the stakeholder's raw sentence. It names a feeling, not a system. Do not design from it directly.
  2. The four question cards: ask in this order. Pain and volume tell you whether the problem is worth solving. The target number tells you what "done" means. The limits remove whole pattern families before you draw anything.
  3. Right (the clear spec): one short written record: pain, volume, target, limits, cost of inaction. Everything from 1.2 onward builds on this spec.
  4. The exam move: when a scenario opens with a vague business request, the credited first step is to ask clarifying questions and set a baseline. It is never an architecture.

The clarifying questions that matter, in the order to ask them:

  1. What is the pain, in plain words? Get the complaint verbatim. Do not translate it yet. The stakeholder's own words keep you honest about what they actually want.
  2. Who feels it, and how often? One person once a month is a different problem from a team 600 times a day. Volume decides whether the fix is worth building at all.
  3. What does "fixed" look like? Push for a number: faster by how much, errors down to what level. This becomes the success number in 1.3.
  4. What are the hard limits? Budget ceiling, latency deadline, data you may not touch, decisions a human must keep. Limits eliminate whole pattern families at a glance.
  5. What happens if we do nothing? If the answer is "not much", the project is not worth building. The exam rewards the architect who says no.

Write the answers down as one short spec: the pain, the volume, the target, the limits. Skip this step and you design in the dark: the four-step method has nothing to measure, and the pattern selector has nothing to select against.

1.2 What "translation" means

Rung 2: the one-paragraph version. Translation turns a business pain ("customers wait too long") into a system shape ("classify each ticket, route it, draft the reply, human approves"). Stakeholders speak in outcomes: money, time, error rates. Architects speak in mechanisms: inputs, model calls, validators, loops.

The exam tests the bridge between those two languages. Most real projects die in this gap. They start from the technology ("let's build an agent"). They do not start from the measurement ("triage takes 9 minutes per ticket and 18% get misrouted").

The rule that fixes it: write the success number before you draw the architecture. A design that cannot name the number it improves is a failed design.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the left (Pain): the raw complaint, in the stakeholder's own words. It is not a design input yet.
  2. Measure: convert the pain into a baseline number (minutes per ticket, error rate, dollars). No baseline means no way to prove the system helped.
  3. Decide: find the decision points in the work. Every place a human reads something and judges something is a candidate for the model.
  4. Pattern: pick the narrowest architectural pattern (Unit 3) that covers the decision points. The pattern comes after the measurement, never before.
  5. Test: the loop closes when the system moves the number from step 2. If it does not move, the translation was wrong, not the model.

1.3 The four-step method

Rung 3: one level deeper. The funnel above is a slogan until you run it. The method is four steps, in order, each producing one artifact you can point at.

1. Find the expensive loop   watch the work: repetition, backlogs, priced errors
2. Write the success number  baseline + target + how you will measure it weekly
3. Find the decision points  judgment moments = model territory; the rest = code
4. Test "AI-shaped?"         messy input? no if-statement? checkable cost? verifier?

Step 1: Find the expensive loop

Watch the work, don't ask about it. Look for repetition (the same reading task done hundreds of times), backlogs (queues that never drain), and errors with a price (misroutes, rework, refunds). The expensive loop is the unit of work you will automate. In support triage the loop is: read ticket, decide category and priority, assign. It repeats 600 times a day.

Step 2: Write the success number first

A success number has three parts: the baseline (where we are), the target (where we must be), and the instrument (how we will measure it weekly). Take this example. "Triage costs 2 minutes of human time per ticket today. Target: under 30 seconds of human time per ticket. Routing accuracy must reach at least 92%. We measure it on a weekly sample of 200 tickets." Without the instrument, the target is a wish.

Step 3: Find the decision points

A decision point is any moment a human reads unstructured input and applies judgment. The human asks things like: is this urgent? Which team owns this? Is this refund allowed by policy?

Each decision point is a moment where the model can do useful work. Everything between decision points is plumbing: databases, queues, templates. Plumbing must be code, not model calls. Code is cheaper and exact.

Step 4: Test whether the task is "AI-shaped"

A task is AI-shaped when four conditions hold. The input is language or messy data, not a clean table. You cannot write the rule as an if-statement. The task needs judgment. A wrong answer has a bounded and checkable cost.

You can spot a wrong answer and fix it. A verifier exists: a human reviewer or a machine check. If the rule can be an if-statement, write the if-statement. The exam loves this. The credited answer is often "no LLM needed, this is a rules engine".

How to read this diagram
  1. The four cards are the four conditions from Unit 1. Read them left to right as a checklist.
  2. Messy input means language or messy data, not a clean table. Clean tables belong to code.
  3. No if-statement means you cannot write the rule as code. If you can, write the code.
  4. Bounded cost means a wrong answer has a checkable cost and a verifier exists. Without a verifier, do not ship.
  5. What breaks: any condition fails and the model is the wrong tool. The exam usually credits "no LLM needed".
How to read this diagram
  1. Read left to right. Each box ends with the artifact it produces: the loop, the number, the judgment map, the go or no-go call.
  2. Step 2 is the hinge: baseline plus target plus a measurement instrument. Without the instrument the target is a wish.
  3. Takeaway: skip a step and the design rests on a slogan. The method turns a vague ask into something you can point at.

1.4 When Claude is NOT the answer

The turn. The method tells you how to translate a problem. It does not tell you when to stop: some problems are not Claude problems at all. This section draws that line.

As you learned in the prereq, Claude makes predictions over tokens. It does not recall facts perfectly, and it cannot enforce guarantees. The three shapes below are the cases where that distinction decides the design.

Rung 4: the full picture. The hardest translation calls end with "no model needed". Learn the three shapes where the model is the wrong tool, and the one design principle that covers them all.

Need perfect recall?      -> search / database, model only summarizes
Need a guarantee?         -> policy gate in CODE; model may suggest, code enforces
Cheap simple high-volume? -> script; a model burns money for zero judgment

Three common shapes where the model is the wrong tool:

  • Perfect recall needed: "find the exact invoice from March." That is search and indexing, not generation. Use retrieval (or a database query) and let the model only summarize what was found.
  • Guarantees needed: "never approve a refund over $500 without a manager." That is a policy gate in code. A model can suggest, code must enforce.
  • Cheap, simple, high-volume transforms: "reformat these 2 million CSV rows." That is a script. Using a model here burns money for zero judgment.

The design principle: put deterministic code where the task is deterministic, put the model where you need judgment. Every model call in your architecture must defend a decision point from step 3. If a call defends no decision point, delete it.

Worked example: support triage, with numbers (illustrative)

A company gets 600 tickets a day. Today a human spends 2 minutes reading and routing each one. Misroutes happen 18% of the time, and each misroute costs 8 minutes of re-handling. The current cost, stated as equations:

600 × 2 = 1,200 minutes (20 hours) of human reading and routing per day
600 × 0.18 × 8 = 864 minutes (14.4 hours) of re-handling per day

where: 600 = tickets per day. 2 = minutes a human spends reading and routing one ticket. 0.18 = misroute rate. 8 = minutes of re-handling per misroute.

Translation: success number = routing accuracy at least 92% (up from 82%), triage human time under 30 seconds per ticket, measured weekly on 200 sampled tickets.

If the system hits 94% accuracy, misroutes fall from 18% to 6%. The saving, worked step by step:

600 × 0.12 × 8 = 576 minutes saved per day

where: 0.12 = the drop in misroute rate (0.18 − 0.06). 600 = tickets per day. 8 = re-handling minutes per misroute.

576 ÷ 60 = 9.6 hours saved daily. At a loaded cost of $25/hour, that is 9.6 × 25 = $240/day. That is about $62,000/year. The model cost for 600 short classification calls a day is on the order of $10–15/day. The translation makes the business case visible before you write a single prompt.

Notice what the numbers chose for us: high volume, a clean decision point, cheap per-call cost. That points at a routing workflow with a small model, not an autonomous agent. The pattern decision fell out of the measurement.

How they will ask this

How to read this diagram
  1. Baseline is where you are: 600 tickets a day, 2 minutes of human time each, 18 percent misrouted.
  2. Target is where you must be: 92 percent routing accuracy, under 30 seconds of human time per ticket.
  3. Success number equals baseline plus target plus instrument: measured weekly on 200 sampled tickets.
  4. What breaks: skipping the instrument. A target nobody measures is a wish, and the pattern choice becomes politics.
Scenario shape: a stakeholder request in business language ("reduce churn", "speed up review") with a cost or time constraint, plus several technical options.

The trap: options that jump to architecture before any baseline or success metric exists. Distractor names to recognize: "fine-tune a model", "deploy an agent swarm", "use the biggest model". Starting from the technology is the trap.

The credited answer defines the baseline and success number first. Then it identifies the decision points. Then it picks the narrowest pattern that meets the constraint. Watch for the "not an LLM problem" variant: when you can write the rule as code, the credited answer is code.

Next: Unit 2, the four stages every system shares: input, processing, output, and the feedback loops that keep the system honest.

How to read this diagram
  1. The three red cards are the three shapes: perfect recall (use search), guarantees (a policy gate in code), cheap high-volume transforms (a script).
  2. The green banner states the covering principle: put deterministic code where the task is deterministic, put the model where you need judgment.
  3. Takeaway: the hardest translation calls end with no model needed. Every model call should defend a decision point. A call defending nothing gets deleted.

Unit 2: End-to-end architectures: input, processing, output, feedback loops

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 1 turned a vague business ask into a measured problem, with accuracy targets, cost ceilings, and latency budgets. A measured problem is still not a system. This unit answers the next question. What does the full system look like around the model call, from raw input to validated output and back again?

On the board.

"Draw the full system for a contract-review assistant, from the PDF landing in the inbox to the lawyer signing off". This question checks that you think about what happens around the model call. That is where production systems fail.

2.1 The four stages

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Every Claude system has the same four stages. This holds from a one-call summarizer to a multi-agent research fleet. Input captures and prepares the raw material. Processing does the thinking: model calls, tools, memory, state.

Output validates and delivers the result. Feedback loops carry what happened back into the system, so it gets better (or at least stops getting worse). The model call is usually the smallest part of the code and the largest part of the risk. A design that only describes the middle stage is not a design.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read left to right: every user request flows Input → Process → Output. That is the hot path. Latency and cost budgets are set here (see the worked example at the end of 2.5, and Unit 6 for the SLA that enforces them).
  2. Input: capture, validate, normalize, redact. Garbage in is not the model's fault. It is an input-stage failure.
  3. Process: the model, its tools, and its working memory. The only stage where judgment happens.
  4. Output: validate the result against a schema or policy, format it for the consumer, then act or present. This stage is the safety boundary.
  5. The return arrow (Learn): production traffic, user corrections, and eval results flow back to improve prompts, retrieval data, and routing. A system with no return arrow is a prototype, not a product.

2.2 Input stage: capture, validate, normalize, redact

Rung 2: one level deeper. Each stage is a small machine with its own jobs. Start with input, because input quality decides what the model can know.

raw world  ->  CAPTURE (get it + its context)  ->  VALIDATE (size, type, shape)
           ->  NORMALIZE (one canonical form)   ->  REDACT (strip secrets + personal data)
           ->  safe, clean material for the model

The input stage turns the messy world into something the model can safely read. Four jobs, in order:

  • Capture: get the data in with its context (who sent it, when, what it relates to). A support ticket without the customer's history is a different task than one with it.
  • Validate: check size, type, and shape before the model ever sees it. Reject a 500 MB "PDF", cap input length, confirm it is actually the expected document type. Validation failures should fail fast and loudly, not become weird model behavior.
  • Normalize: convert formats, languages, and encodings into one canonical form. Two tickets saying the same thing in different words should look the same to the model. This is also where you attach retrieved context (the RAG step, retrieval-augmented generation: fetching relevant documents and feeding them into the prompt before the processing stage).
  • Redact: strip secrets, credentials, and personal data the model does not need. The model cannot leak what it never saw. Redaction is a privacy control. On this exam it is often the difference between a compliant design and a failing one.

Under the hood, the input stage is almost entirely code, not model calls. That is the point: code is exact, cheap, and testable. Reserve the model for judgment.

How to read this diagram
  1. Follow the arrows left to right. Raw world in. Capture with context. Validate size, type, and shape. Normalize to one form. Redact secrets and personal data.
  2. The banner states the ordering rule: validate before the model ever sees it, and fail fast and loudly instead of producing weird model behavior.
  3. Takeaway: the model cannot leak what it never saw. Redaction is a privacy control, not a cleanup step.

2.3 Processing stage: the model, its tools, and its state

Processing is where judgment happens. Three ingredients:

MODEL CALL (stateless: everything it knows is in the prompt)
   + TOOLS (its hands: narrow schemas, explicit contracts)
   + STATE (what persists: history, task list, scratchpad)
   = one thinking step; loop as needed
  • Model calls arranged in one of the Unit 3 patterns. The call is stateless: everything the model knows about this request must be in the prompt (system prompt, conversation, retrieved context, tool results). There is no hidden memory between calls unless you build it.
  • Tools are the model's hands: APIs, databases, search, code execution. A tool call is a contract: the model supplies arguments matching a schema, the tool returns observations. Design tools with narrow, explicit schemas. A tool that can "do anything" is a tool the model will misuse.
  • State is what persists across calls and turns: conversation history, a task list, a scratchpad, a database row. State design answers two questions: what does the model need to remember, and what happens when it is wrong (stale state is a classic production bug).

A key under-the-hood fact: each model call pays for its full input every time (minus caching). A 10-turn conversation re-sends the earlier turns on every call. Long state therefore has a direct, linear cost, which is why Unit 5's decomposition and Unit 4's context isolation exist.

How to read this diagram
  1. The three cards are the ingredients: a stateless model call, tools with narrow schemas, and state that persists across calls.
  2. All three feed the green box: one thinking step, looped as needed. There is no hidden memory between calls unless you build it.
  3. Takeaway: each call pays for its full input every time, so a 10-turn conversation re-bills the whole history on every turn.

2.4 Output stage: validate, format, act

Never let raw model text trigger a real-world action. The output stage is the safety boundary, with three jobs:

model text  ->  VALIDATE (schema? policy? confident enough?)
            ->  FORMAT (human-readable or exact JSON, per consumer)
            ->  ACT or PRESENT (log it; high stakes get a human gate)
  • Validate: check the model's output against a schema (did it return the fields we need?), against policy (does policy allow the action?), and against confidence (is the model sure enough for an irreversible step?). A refund over a threshold, a database write, an email to a customer: these need explicit allowlists (a list of actions the system may take; the system blocks anything not listed), not vibes.
  • Format: shape the result for its consumer. A human wants a readable summary with sources. A downstream API wants JSON with exact keys. Formatting is code's job.
  • Act or present: either take the action (with logging) or present the result for approval. High-stakes actions get a human approval gate. Low-stakes reversible actions can auto-apply with an audit trail.

The exam's favorite failure: an agent that acts directly on model output with no validation step. When you see that in a scenario, the credited fix is almost always "add output validation, an allowlist, or a human gate". It is never "use a bigger model".

How to read this diagram
  1. Follow the arrows: model text enters, validation checks schema policy and confidence, formatting shapes it for the consumer, then it acts or reaches the consumer.
  2. High-stakes actions get a human gate. Formatting is code's job, never the model's.
  3. Takeaway: the red banner names the exam's favorite failure, an agent acting on raw model output. The credited fix is always a validation step.

2.5 Feedback loops: the system that keeps the system honest

Rung 3: the full picture. A model never stops meeting new inputs, so behavior drifts even when code does not change. Four loops fight the drift, each on its own clock:

PRODUCT loop  (hours-days):    user signals -> prompt tweaks, routing rules
EVAL loop     (weekly):        golden-set reruns -> catch regressions early
DATA loop     (monthly):       production examples -> better corpora, examples
HUMAN loop    (continuous):    sampled review -> catches what metrics miss
  • Product loop (fast, hours to days): user signals: thumbs up/down, corrections, "that was wrong" clicks. Feeds prompt tweaks and routing rules.
  • Eval loop (medium, weekly): re-run a golden set (a fixed set of test cases with known-good answers) on every prompt or model change. Catches regressions before users do. This is the loop D4 owns. D1 must design the hooks for it (log inputs, outputs, and decisions).
  • Data loop (slow, monthly to quarterly): production examples become training signal: better retrieval corpora, fine-tuning data, few-shot examples (a few example inputs and outputs placed in the prompt so the model copies the pattern). Slow because it needs volume and cleaning.
  • Human loop (safety, continuous sampling): humans review a sample of outputs, especially edge cases and high-stakes actions. Catches what metrics miss: tone problems, novel failure modes, drift the golden set does not cover.

The diagram below is from Anthropic's own engineering writing. It shows an agent in a tight sense-act-observe loop with a human and an environment. The loop: clarify until the task is clear. Act through tools. Observe results. Iterate until tests pass.

Every arrow in it is a feedback loop at a different timescale. The design lesson: the loops make the system reliable, not the single call.

How to read this diagram
  1. Product loop (hours to days): user signals feed prompt tweaks and routing rules.
  2. Eval loop (weekly): the golden set re-runs on every prompt or model change and catches regressions.
  3. Data loop (monthly to quarterly): production examples become better retrieval and training data.
  4. Human loop (sampling): humans review edge cases and catch what metrics miss.
  5. What breaks: a system with no return arrow is a prototype, not a product.

How to read this diagram
  1. Columns are actors: Human, Interface, LLM, Environment. Time flows downward; every horizontal arrow is one interaction.
  2. Top loop ("Until tasks clear"): the human and the model clarify and refine the request. This is the product loop at conversation scale: the team clears ambiguity before expensive work starts.
  3. Middle exchange ("Send context", "Search files", "Return paths"): the model pulls in real information through tools instead of guessing. Retrieval before reasoning.
  4. Bottom loop ("Until tests pass"): the model writes code, runs tests, reads results, and iterates. This is the tightest feedback loop: the environment itself is the validator, no human needed.
  5. The design takeaway: reliability comes from loops with checks (clarify, search, test), not from one brilliant call. When a scenario lacks a check between steps, that missing loop is the flaw to name.
Worked example: latency and cost budget per stage (illustrative)

A RAG support-answer system with a 5-second p95 latency SLA (p95: the latency that 95% of requests beat. It measures the slow tail, not the average). The budget, per request:
Stage What happens Latency budget Cost driver
Input Validate, redact, turn the query into a search vector (an embedding), retrieve 5 chunks 600 ms Embedding + vector search (cheap)
Processing One model call: ~1,800 input tokens, ~400 output tokens 3,000 ms Tokens in + out (the big one)
Output Schema check, citation verification, format 400 ms Code (near free)
Total 4,000 ms (1,000 ms headroom under the 5 s SLA) About $0.01–0.02 per query at published list prices

Two lessons the exam rewards. First, the model call dominates both latency and cost, so you must justify every extra call against the SLA. Second, the 1,000 ms headroom is not waste: it absorbs retrieval slowdowns and model variance. A design with zero headroom fails the SLA on a busy day.

A natural question: where do retries and fallbacks live?

In the seams between stages. If the model call times out, the processing stage retries once with a shorter prompt or falls back to a smaller model. If retrieval returns nothing, the input stage flags low-confidence context and the output stage adds a disclaimer or routes to a human. Fallback logic is part of the architecture, not an afterthought: each stage declares what it does when its dependency fails.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: a system description with a stage missing or broken: no input validation (prompt injection, malicious input that tries to override the system's instructions, walks in), no output validation (agent emails customers directly), no logging (evals impossible later).

The trap: fixing the model (bigger model, more prompting) when the failure is in the plumbing around it. Name the missing stage or loop: add input redaction, add an output allowlist, add logging hooks for the eval loop. Read the scenario for where it breaks, not which model it uses. Note the anti-retraining point above. When a scenario asks how a system stays accurate over time, the credited answers are the fast loops: logging, evals, human sampling. The answer is not a retraining pipeline.

Next: Unit 3, the three pattern families (augmented LLM, workflows, agents) and the selection rule that picks among them.

Unit 3: The three pattern families: augmented LLM, workflows, agents

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 2 gave you four stages that every system shares. It left one question open: who controls the path through those stages, deterministic code or the model itself? This unit answers with the three pattern families: augmented LLM, workflows, and agents.

On the board.

"Here is a task with fixed steps and a tight cost budget. Here is an open-ended research task. Which pattern for each, and what breaks if you swap them?" This is the most-tested idea in D1. Learn the selection rule cold.

3.1 The spectrum, in one paragraph

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Picture a slider. At one end: workflows, where code defines the path and the model handles the steps. At the other: agents, where the model plans its own path and uses tools to act. Between them sit the augmented LLM building blocks (retrieval, tools, memory) that both sides use.

Anthropic's "Building Effective Agents" (the engineering essay this whole unit follows) gives the core advice. Start with the simplest pattern that can work, and add complexity only when it measurably improves the outcome. Most exam traps are designs that start at the complex end.

3.2 The building block: the augmented LLM

Rung 2: one level deeper. Before patterns, the atom. An augmented LLM is a model call with superpowers attached: retrieval (look up facts instead of guessing), tools (call APIs, run code, search), and memory (read and write notes across turns). The model still runs once per request.

The augmentation just gives that one call better inputs and real actions. If your task fits in one augmented call, stop here. Every pattern below adds calls, latency, cost, and failure modes.

request in  ->  [ RETRIEVAL: query/index/results ]
                [ TOOLS:      call/response      ]  ->  one MODEL call  ->  answer out
                [ MEMORY:     read/write notes  ]

How to read this diagram
  1. Top row (In → LLM → Out): a single model call. No orchestration, no loops, no second agent. This is the simplest possible LLM system.
  2. The three dashed arrows below: the augmentations. Retrieval answers "Query/Results" (the model asks, the index answers). Tools answer "Call/Response" (the model invokes a function, gets an observation). Memory answers "Read/Write" (notes persist across turns).
  3. Why it matters: if your task fits in one augmented call, stop here. Every pattern below adds calls, latency, cost, and failure modes. The exam rewards the designer who can defend not building more.

3.3 Workflows: code owns the path

Rung 2, continued: the workflow family. In a workflow, code fixes the steps and their order. The model contributes judgment inside steps, but it never decides what happens next. Workflows win on three axes: predictability (you can trace and test every path), cost (fixed number of calls), and debuggability (when step 2 fails, you know it was step 2). Use a workflow whenever the task's steps are known in advance. Five workflow patterns cover nearly everything:

Pattern A: Prompt chaining

Decompose the task into a fixed sequence of calls. Each call's output feeds the next. Outline → draft → edit. Extract → summarize → format.

Under the hood, the win is checkpoints. You can validate each step's output before the next step consumes it. Validation catches errors early instead of letting them compound through one giant call. Each step can also use a different model or prompt tuned to that subtask. The cost is N small calls instead of one big one, which is often cheaper because each call carries a focused prompt. Latency is the sum of the steps unless independent steps run in parallel.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read left to right: each box is one model call with its own prompt. Arrows show the output of one becoming the input of the next.
  2. The checkpoints between boxes are where your code validates the handoff (schema check, quality gate). This is the reliability mechanism: bad output from step 1 never silently poisons step 3.
  3. What breaks: if a middle step's output drifts in format, every downstream step fails. Fix with strict output schemas per step, not with a bigger model.
How to read this diagram
  1. The three boxes show fixed steps: extract, flag, draft. Code owns the path, not the model.
  2. The gray validate gates check each step's output before the next step runs.
  3. Best when the task splits into clean sequential subtasks with a cheap check between steps.
  4. What breaks: a missing validator. One bad handoff poisons every step after it.

Pattern B: Routing

Classify the input, then send it to a specialist: a different prompt, a different model, or a different tool. Support tickets go to billing, technical, or refunds handlers. Easy questions go to a small cheap model. Hard ones escalate.

Under the hood, the router is the cheapest component that can classify reliably. Sometimes it is a small model. Sometimes it is embeddings plus a classifier. Sometimes it is rules for the obvious cases. The economic win is blended cost.

If 80% of traffic is easy and the small model costs one-tenth of the big one, routing cuts the model bill dramatically. The 20% hard cases still get full quality. The risk is misrouting: a hard question sent to the weak model fails. The router's accuracy is the system's accuracy ceiling for the easy path. Measure the router separately.

Concrete numbers (illustrative): 10,000 queries a day, 2,000 input tokens per query. Big model at $3 per million input tokens, small model at $0.25. Routed 80/20 with 95% router accuracy:

all big: 10,000 × 2,000 × $3/1M = $60/day
routed: (8,000 × 2,000 × $0.25/1M) + (2,000 × 2,000 × $3/1M) = $4 + $12 = $16/day

where: 10,000 = queries per day. 2,000 = input tokens per query. $3/1M and $0.25/1M = big and small model input prices. 80/20 = share of easy vs hard queries.

Worked: the easy 8,000 queries cost 8,000 × 2,000 = 16M tokens × $0.25/1M = $4. The hard 2,000 cost 2,000 × 2,000 = 4M tokens × $3/1M = $12. Total $16/day: same quality on the hard 20%, roughly one-quarter the $60/day all-big cost.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left box (input): every request enters the same door.
  2. The router diamond: one classification decision. It must be cheap and accurate. Log every routing decision so you can audit misroutes.
  3. The specialist lanes: different prompts, models, or tools per class. The lanes are independent, so you can tune, test, and cost each lane separately.
  4. What breaks: a new input type the router never saw gets forced into the wrong lane. Fix with a fallback lane (human review or the big model) for low-confidence classifications.
How to read this diagram
  1. The router diamond is one classification decision. It must be cheap and accurate.
  2. The green lane is the small model: 80 percent of easy traffic at one-tenth the cost.
  3. The amber lane is the big model: the 20 percent of hard cases that earn full quality.
  4. What breaks: misrouting. A hard question sent to the weak model fails, so log every routing decision and audit the misses.

Pattern C: Parallelization

Run subtasks at the same time and combine the results. Two flavors:

  • Sectioning: split one task into independent pieces, run each piece, merge. One call per report section. One call per document chunk. Guardrails where one model instance checks another's section. Latency becomes the slowest piece, not the sum.
  • Voting: run the same task N times and pick the best or the majority answer. Costs N times more, but crushes variance on tasks where any single call might fumble. Works when outputs are checkable (code that must pass tests, answers with a clear rubric).

Under the hood, sectioning needs the pieces to be truly independent: shared context between pieces reintroduces coupling. Voting needs a selection rule decided in advance: majority vote, best-of-N by a scorer, or first output that passes a validator. The exam-relevant math: if one call is right 80% of the time, the majority of 5 independent calls is right about 94% (binomial: probability at least 3 of 5 succeed). You pay 5× the calls to buy 14 points of reliability. Say that trade explicitly when you choose voting.

How to read this diagram
  1. The fan-out: one input splits into parallel calls. In sectioning each call gets a different piece. In voting each call gets the same task.
  2. The parallel boxes: they run simultaneously, so wall-clock latency is the slowest box, not the total. This is the speed argument.
  3. The merge: an aggregator combines results. For sectioning it concatenates or synthesizes. For voting it applies the pre-decided selection rule.
  4. What breaks: pieces that secretly depend on each other (merge produces contradictions), or a merge step with no conflict-resolution rule. Define the merge logic in code, not in a prompt.

Pattern D: Orchestrator-workers

A central model breaks the task into subtasks, delegates each to a worker model, and synthesizes the results. The orchestrator plans. The workers execute. This is the pattern behind coding agents (plan the change, spawn workers per file) and research systems (plan the questions, spawn researchers per question).

Under the hood, the killer feature is context isolation. Each worker gets a fresh context window containing only its subtask. Workers never get lost in each other's details. The orchestrator only sees summaries.

This beats one giant context window because of the "lost in the middle" effect (models attend worse to the middle of long contexts) and because per-worker prompts stay focused. Cost: one orchestrator call plus N worker calls, all with their own tools. More in Unit 4.

How to read this diagram
  1. Top box (orchestrator): receives the task, decomposes it, and defines each worker's assignment. It never does the detailed work itself.
  2. The worker row: each worker is an independent model call with its own context and tools. Workers do not talk to each other. All coordination flows through the orchestrator.
  3. The synthesis arrow back up: the orchestrator merges worker outputs into the final answer. Give the orchestrator explicit merge instructions (dedupe, resolve conflicts, cite sources).
  4. What breaks: vague worker assignments (workers duplicate or miss work) and unbounded delegation (workers spawning workers). Cap the fan-out and the depth.

Pattern E: Evaluator-optimizer

One model generates, another evaluates, and the loop repeats until the output passes. Write → critique → rewrite. Translate → check → fix. The loop needs a clear stop condition: a pass/fail criterion, plus a maximum iteration cap so it cannot spin forever.

Under the hood, this pattern works when evaluation is easier than generation. It is easier to check a translation than to produce one. It is easier to run tests than to write correct code. The evaluator can be a model, a rubric, or code (a test suite is the perfect evaluator).

Typical loops converge in 2–4 rounds. Budget for the cap (say 5) in cost and latency math. The failure mode is evaluator-model collusion in spirit: a weak evaluator approves everything, so the loop adds cost without adding quality. Test the evaluator independently.

How to read this diagram
  1. Generate is one model writing. Evaluate is the quality gate: a rubric, a test suite, or a checklist.
  2. The red loop-back returns rejected output with the evaluator's feedback attached.
  3. The cap is the stop condition plus a maximum iteration count. Typical loops converge in 2 to 4 rounds.
  4. What breaks: a weak evaluator approves everything. The loop then adds cost without adding quality, so test the evaluator independently.

How to read this diagram
  1. Generator box: produces a candidate answer. It favors fluency and coverage, not correctness.
  2. Evaluator diamond: the quality gate. It applies the pass criterion: a rubric, a test suite, or a checklist. This is the most important box in the diagram.
  3. The loop-back arrow: rejected output returns with the evaluator's feedback attached. Cap the loops (a fixed maximum) so cost stays bounded.
  4. What breaks: a vague pass criterion (the loop never converges) or no cap (cost explodes on hard inputs). Both are design decisions, not model problems.

3.4 Agents: the model owns the path

Rung 3: the full picture. An agent is a model in a loop. It gathers context, takes actions through tools, observes the results, and repeats until it decides the task is done. Nobody told it the steps.

It plans, tries, errs, and recovers. This is the right pattern when the number and order of steps cannot be known in advance. Three examples: open-ended research, debugging an unfamiliar codebase, booking a trip with shifting constraints.

goal + history  ->  MODEL picks next action  ->  TOOL acts on environment
       ^                                              |
       +----  observation returns, history grows  ----+
until: stop condition met (tests pass / cited answer / step cap hit)

Under the hood, the agent's action space is its tool list, and its "brain" is the conversation history accumulating tool observations. Three design problems dominate:

  • Stop conditions: the agent must recognize "done". Without explicit completion criteria (tests pass, answer cites sources, max N steps reached), agents ramble or loop. Always set a step cap and a success check.
  • Unpredictable cost: one task might take 3 tool calls, the next 40. Budget for the cap, monitor per-task spend, and require approval for expensive or irreversible actions.
  • Debuggability: when an agent fails, the failure is a 30-step story, not a single bad step. Full trace logging (every thought, tool call, and observation) is not optional. It is how you diagnose anything.

How to read this diagram
  1. Center (LLM): the model is the controller now, not a step in someone else's code. It reads the goal and the history, then chooses the next action.
  2. The tool/environment arrows: actions go out (search, read, write, run), observations come back and append to the model's context. The loop is the whole system.
  3. The missing piece to design: the stop condition and the guardrails (step caps, approval gates, allowed tools). The diagram shows the loop. Your architecture must show the brakes.
  4. What breaks: unclear goals (the agent optimizes the wrong thing), too many tools (the agent misuses them), no logging (failures are mysteries). Constrain all three.

3.5 The selection rule

Rung 3, the exam rung: the decision procedure. Memorize this. It answers a large share of D1 items:

  1. Can you list the steps in advance? Yes → workflow. No → consider an agent.
  2. Is there a cheap check between steps? Yes → chaining or evaluator-optimizer with validators. No → keep the design simpler, not more complex.
  3. Does input variety demand different handling? Yes → routing. Distinct input classes with distinct needs are the routing trigger.
  4. Are subtasks independent? Yes → parallelization (sectioning for speed, voting for reliability).
  5. Is the task too big for one context? Yes → orchestrator-workers with context isolation (Unit 4).
  6. Is the path unknowable upfront? Yes → agent, with step caps, approval gates, and full tracing.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the top diamond: answer each question honestly about the task, not about the technology you want to use.
  2. Follow the branch: "steps known?" leads toward workflows. "path unknowable?" leads toward agents. "judgment not needed?" leads away from the model entirely (code).
  3. The lanes at the bottom are the pattern families. Landing in a lane means that family is the narrowest sufficient choice. You may still add one augmentation (retrieval, a validator) without changing lanes.
  4. The exam move: when a scenario's constraint is cost, determinism, or auditability, the tree almost always lands on a workflow. Agents win only when the scenario stresses open-endedness or unknown step counts.
Pattern Determinism Cost shape Latency shape Best for
Augmented LLM (single call) High (one call) Fixed, lowest One call Answer-with-context tasks: Q&A, summarization, classification
Prompt chaining High Fixed: N small calls Sum of steps Clean sequential subtasks with checkable handoffs
Routing High Blended: cheap for easy, full for hard Router + specialist Distinct input classes with different needs or costs
Parallelization High Fixed: N calls (voting multiplies) Slowest piece Independent pieces (sectioning) or variance reduction (voting)
Orchestrator-workers Medium Orchestrator + N workers Slowest worker + synthesis Big tasks needing fresh context per subtask
Evaluator-optimizer Medium Bounded by iteration cap Rounds × call time Tasks where checking is easier than doing
Autonomous agent Low Unpredictable: budget the cap Unpredictable: budget the cap Open-ended tasks with unknowable step counts
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: a task description with clues about step predictability, input variety, and constraints (cost ceiling, latency SLA, auditability). Options name the patterns.

The trap: picking the autonomous agent for a well-understood task ("it can handle anything") or picking a rigid workflow for an open-ended task ("it is cheaper"). Agents are not the advanced version of workflows. They are a different tool for a different uncertainty level.

The credited answer matches the pattern to the uncertainty: known steps → workflow. Varied inputs → routing. Independent pieces → parallelization. Unknowable path → agent with caps and gates. For multiple-response items, expect "select two": often the pattern plus its essential guardrail (e.g., evaluator-optimizer and an iteration cap).

How to read this diagram
  1. Read each row as signal on the left, narrowest sufficient pattern on the right.
  2. Known steps mean workflow. Varied inputs mean routing. Checkable quality means evaluator-optimizer.
  3. Unknowable path means agent, but only with caps and gates. The guardrail is part of the answer.
  4. What breaks: picking the agent for a well-understood task, or a rigid workflow for an open-ended one.

Next: Unit 4, multi-agent systems: harness versus swarm, the four topologies, and context isolation under the hood.

Unit 4: Multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 3 placed agents at the powerful end of the spectrum, where the model owns the path. That raises a new problem: one agent can only do so much before its context dilutes and its errors compound. This unit answers how several agents work together without tripping over each other.

On the board.

"We need to research 50 vendors in parallel and produce one ranked shortlist. One big agent or many small ones? Who coordinates, and what stops them from doing the same work twice?" Multi-agent design is orchestration design.

4.1 What "multi-agent" actually means

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. A multi-agent system is more than one model-driven actor working on one goal, with defined roles and communication paths. The actors are usually subagents: worker agents spawned by a main agent, each with its own context window, its own tools, and a narrow assignment. When a worker finishes, it returns a summary to whoever spawned it.

main agent: "research 50 vendors, give me one ranked list"
   |-- spawns --> subagent A: vendors 1-17   (own window, own tools)
   |-- spawns --> subagent B: vendors 18-34  (own window, own tools)
   |-- spawns --> subagent C: vendors 35-50  (own window, own tools)
   +-- collects summaries, synthesizes one shortlist

Why it exists: three pressures that one agent cannot solve alone. Context pressure: a single conversation window fills up and the model loses track (the "lost in the middle" effect, where attention to the middle of long contexts degrades). Parallelism pressure: independent subtasks should run at the same time. Specialization pressure: different subtasks need different prompts, tools, and instructions, and stuffing them all into one prompt dilutes each.

How to read this diagram
  1. Solid blue arrows mean spawning: the main agent hands each subagent a narrow assignment with its own window and tools.
  2. Dashed gray arrows are the return path: workers send back summaries, and the main agent synthesizes one shortlist.
  3. Takeaway: the green banner gives the three pressures one agent cannot solve, context pressure, parallelism pressure, and specialization pressure.

4.2 Harness vs swarm: the two coordination philosophies

Rung 2: one level deeper. Once you have many actors, someone must coordinate them. There are two philosophies, and the exam wants you to pick between them.

HARNESS (top-down, the default)        SWARM (bottom-up, the exception)

     [orchestrator]                       A <--> B
      /    |    \                        ^ \ / ^
     A     B     C                       |  X  |
  (workers see only                   C <--> D
   their assignment)                  no center; peers hand off

Harness (top-down): one orchestrator agent plans the work, spawns subagents, collects their results, and synthesizes. The orchestrator holds the global state. Subagents are stateless workers that see only their assignment. Anthropic built its own research system as a top-down harness. This guide treats the harness as the default starting point. It is debuggable: every decision about who does what is visible in one place.

Swarm (bottom-up): peer agents hand work to each other directly, with no central controller. Agent A finishes its part and decides Agent B should take the next step. This is flexible when nobody knows the right structure in advance, but it has two costs.

First, coordination grows with the square of the agent count. With n agents, there are n×(n−1)/2 possible pairwise channels. In practice you get duplicate work, conflicting actions, and emergent loops. Second, debugging is spread out: no single place decided anything.

The exam rule of thumb: pick the harness unless the scenario explicitly demands emergent, peer-to-peer behavior. "More autonomous" is not "better architected".

How to read this diagram
  1. Left panel: one orchestrator holds the global state and spawns workers that see only their assignment. Debuggable because every decision is visible in one place.
  2. Right panel: peer agents hand off directly through a dashed web of channels. No center, so coordination grows as n times n minus 1 over 2.
  3. Takeaway: default to the harness. Reach for the swarm only when you must discover the structure itself.

4.3 Topologies: four shapes and when each wins

How to read this diagram
  1. Left (hub): one large central node connected to satellites. The center plans and synthesizes. Satellites execute in isolated contexts. Use for research, coding, analysis: any task that decomposes into parallel subtasks with one final answer.
  2. Middle (pipeline): nodes in a chain with arrows. Each stage transforms the output of the last. Use for staged processing with fixed handoffs (ingest → extract → validate → publish). This is prompt chaining with agents at each step.
  3. Right (swarm): a mesh with no center. Use only when the right decomposition is unknown and must emerge, and accept the debugging cost.
  4. The missing fourth shape (hierarchical): hubs within hubs, like an org chart. Use when the problem has natural levels (company → departments → teams). Each level's orchestrator sees only summaries from below.
  5. What breaks in each: hub, vague assignments and unbounded fan-out. Pipeline, a failed middle stage with no retry rule. Swarm, duplicate work and conflicting actions. Name the mitigation in your answer.

4.4 Subagents and context isolation, under the hood

Rung 3: the full picture. This is the mechanism that makes multi-agent systems worth their cost. A context window belongs to a conversation, not to a system. When the main agent spawns a subagent, the subagent starts with a fresh, empty window containing only its assignment. It can read 50,000 tokens of vendor documentation without polluting the main agent's window. When it finishes, only its summary (say 2,000 tokens) returns.

Main agent window (stays small and focused)
|
|-- spawns --> Subagent A window: [assignment A + 50K tokens of docs]
|                returns: 2K-token summary -------+
|-- spawns --> Subagent B window: [assignment B + 50K tokens of docs]  |
|                returns: 2K-token summary ---------------+  |
|-- spawns --> Subagent C window: [assignment C + 50K tokens of docs]  |  |
                 returns: 2K-token summary ---------------+--+--+
                                                            v  v
Main agent sees: 3 summaries (~6K tokens), never the 150K raw tokens

Concrete numbers (illustrative): a vendor-research task touches 150,000 tokens of source material. One agent reading it all pays 150K input tokens in one window and reasons poorly over the middle. Three subagents each read 50K in their own windows (same 150K total tokens, so the token bill is similar), but the main agent's window holds only 6K of summaries. You did not buy fewer tokens.

You bought better attention. That is the trade the exam wants you to articulate: multi-agent is a quality and parallelism play, not a cost-saving play. Total tokens usually go up.

Two more under-the-hood facts. First, subagents do not share memory: if worker A learns something worker B needs, the orchestrator must pass it. Design the handoff explicitly. Second, spawning is not free: each subagent pays its own system prompt and assignment tokens, so fan-out has a fixed overhead per worker. Ten workers doing tiny jobs can cost more in overhead than they save.

How to read this diagram
  1. The blue box is the main agent window: small, focused, never touching the 150K raw tokens.
  2. Amber windows do the heavy reading, 50K tokens of docs each. The teal boxes are all that returns: a 2K-token summary per worker.
  3. Takeaway: same total token bill, but the main agent reasons over 6K clean tokens instead of 150K noisy ones. That is why multi-agent wins.

4.5 What Anthropic's multi-agent research found

From theory to evidence. Topologies are opinions until you measure them. Here is what Anthropic found when they tested multi-agent systems on real tasks.

Anthropic's engineering team built a multi-agent research system (an orchestrator spawning parallel subagents with their own tools and context windows) and reported the results on their engineering blog. The headline: on their internal research eval, the multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 as lead, Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2%. (Their BrowseComp analysis is separate. In it, token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance.) The gap came from parallel exploration (many lines of inquiry at once) plus context isolation (each researcher kept a clean window). A single orchestrator coordinated the work and synthesized the findings.

The exam-relevant lessons from that work, not just the score:

  • One-shot delegation beats chatty coordination: give each subagent a complete, self-contained assignment. Subagents that must ask clarifying questions mid-task create coordination drag.
  • Parallel tool use multiplies throughput: subagents acting simultaneously explore far more ground per minute than one agent acting in sequence.
  • The orchestrator's synthesis is the quality bottleneck: ten great research reports merged badly produce a bad answer. Invest prompt effort in the merge step: dedupe, resolve conflicts, demand citations.
  • Caps everywhere: cap the number of subagents, cap their steps, cap their tokens. Unbounded delegation is how a research task becomes a runaway bill.
How to read this diagram
  1. The headline: on Anthropic's internal research eval, the multi-agent system beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2 percent.
  2. The three cards are the lessons the exam tests. One-shot delegation beats chatty coordination. Parallel tool use multiplies throughput. The orchestrator's synthesis is the quality bottleneck.
  3. Takeaway: ten great researchers plus one weak synthesizer equals a weak result.

4.6 Failure modes and their mitigations
Failure mode What it looks like Mitigation
Duplicate work Two subagents research the same vendor Partition assignments explicitly. Give each worker a unique slice (by vendor, by region, by question)
Conflicting actions Two agents write to the same record differently Single-writer rule per resource. Orchestrator owns all writes, workers only propose
Runaway delegation Workers spawn workers. Cost explodes Max depth (e.g., workers cannot spawn), max fan-out, per-task token budget
Silent divergence A worker misreads its assignment and nobody notices Workers return structured summaries with confidence. Orchestrator validates against the assignment
Irreversible side effects A subagent sends the email, deletes the row Approval gates: workers propose actions, orchestrator (or human) approves. Allowlists per tool
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: a broad task (research 50 vendors, review 200 contracts, migrate 30 services) with a deadline and a quality bar. Options include: one giant agent with a huge context, a swarm of peers, or an orchestrator-workers harness.

Exam trap.

The trap: the single giant agent (context dilution: it will lose the middle and reason poorly) or the swarm (sounds flexible, but coordination cost and duplicate work have no bound). "More subagents" is not "better": each adds coordination overhead, token overhead, and a new failure surface. The right number is the smallest that covers the task's real parallelism.

The credited answer is the harness: orchestrator decomposes, subagents work in isolated contexts, synthesis is explicit, and you cap fan-out, depth, and token budgets. For multiple-response items, pair the topology with its guardrail: "orchestrator-workers and a max subagent cap" is a classic credited pair. One under-the-hood fact to carry into every answer: subagents do not share the main agent's memory. Every fact that must cross the boundary crosses in a summary you designed.

Next: Unit 5, decomposition techniques: the moves that split a complex problem into pieces with clean boundaries.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read each row left to right: the red or amber card is what the failure looks like, the white card is the mitigation.
  2. Memorize them as pairs: duplicate work with partition explicitly, conflicting actions with the single-writer rule, runaway delegation with depth and budget caps.
  3. Takeaway: the exam's trap answers are the single giant agent (context dilution) and the swarm (unbounded coordination). The credited pick is orchestrator-workers.

Unit 5: Decomposition techniques for complex problems

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 4 showed how to coordinate agents, but it assumed you already knew how to carve the work up. Splitting one complex problem into pieces with clean boundaries is its own skill. This unit teaches the decomposition moves.

On the board.

"The input is a 200-page contract and the question needs five different kinds of judgment. One call or many? How do you split it, and what could go wrong at the seams?" Decomposition is how you make hard problems fit inside reliable pieces.

5.1 Why decompose: the three enemies

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Big tasks break models in three predictable ways. Decomposition is the fix for all three, and the exam tests whether you can name the enemy before you prescribe the split.

CONTEXT DILUTION   long input  -> attention thins, middle gets lost
ERROR COMPOUNDING  one big call -> early misread poisons everything, no checkpoint
INSTRUCTION OVERLOAD  five jobs in one prompt -> each job done worse
        |
        v
ONE CALL, ONE DECISION, ONE CHECKABLE OUTPUT
  • Context dilution: attention spreads thin over long inputs. The model handles the beginning and end of a long context better than the middle ("lost in the middle"). A 130,000-token contract in one call gets worse judgment per clause than forty 4,000-token sections.
  • Error compounding: in one giant call, an early misreading poisons everything downstream with no checkpoint to catch it. Split calls let you validate between steps.
  • Instruction overload: one prompt carrying five different jobs ("extract dates, flag risky clauses, summarize, check compliance, draft the email") does each job worse than five focused prompts. Each added instruction dilutes the others.

The decomposition principle: one call, one decision, one checkable output. When a call does exactly one well-defined thing, you can test it, measure it, price it, and replace it.

How to read this diagram
  1. Each card names one enemy and how it breaks a big call. Attention thins over long input. An early misread poisons everything. Five jobs in one prompt each get done worse.
  2. The green banner states the decomposition principle: one call, one decision, one checkable output.
  3. Takeaway: name the enemy before you prescribe the split. That is what the exam is testing.

5.2 The decomposition moves

Rung 2: one level deeper. Four moves. Learn the trigger for each: the exam describes the task shape, and the shape names the move.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left (the big task): the undecomposed problem. One call, one giant prompt, all three enemies from 5.1 at full strength.
  2. Top branch (split by data): you divide the input and the same operation runs on each piece in parallel. This is sectioning from Unit 3. The split must follow decision boundaries (see 5.4), not arbitrary character counts.
  3. Bottom branch (split by task): you divide the job into sequential steps with different prompts. This is prompt chaining. The next step runs only after validation checks the current step's output.
  4. The exam move: when a scenario has both a huge input and multiple judgment types, the credited design splits twice. Split by data first: parallel workers per section. Split by task second: extract → assess → summarize per section. Say both splits explicitly.

The four moves, precisely:

  • Split by task: divide the job by the kind of thinking required. Classify, then extract, then summarize. Each step gets its own prompt and can use its own model tier (cheap classifier, strong summarizer).
  • Split by data: divide the input and run the same operation on each piece. By document, by section, by record, by time window. Pieces run in parallel. Results merge.
  • Split by question (fan-out): turn one ambiguous question into sub-questions, answer each, synthesize. "Is this vendor safe?" becomes financials, security posture, legal history, references: four focused inquiries, one judgment.
  • Recurse: if a piece is still too big or too mixed, split it again. The stopping rule: a piece fits one clean prompt with one decision and one checkable output. Recursion needs a depth cap, or "split until small" becomes "split forever".

5.3 Sectioning vs voting, precisely

Rung 3: the full picture. Both are parallelization, but they buy different things. Sectioning buys speed and focus: independent pieces, latency of the slowest piece, cost of one pass. Use it when the pieces do not depend on each other. Voting buys reliability: the same task N times, majority or best-of-N wins. Use it when a single call's variance is the risk and outputs are checkable.

The voting math the exam expects you to reason about works like this. If one call succeeds with probability p, the majority of 5 succeeds when at least 3 of 5 succeed. At p = 0.80, that is about 0.94. So 5× the cost buys roughly 14 points of reliability.

The honest version of the same math: at p = 0.55, majority-of-5 only reaches about 0.59, so voting barely helps a near-random base. Voting amplifies an already-decent call. It does not rescue a bad one. And the independence assumption matters: if all 5 calls share the same flawed retrieved context, they fail together and the math collapses.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left panel: independent pieces run in parallel and merge. Latency is the slowest piece, cost is one pass. Use it when pieces do not depend on each other.
  2. Right panel: the same task runs five times and the majority wins. At p equals 0.80 the majority reaches about 0.94, but at p equals 0.55 it only reaches about 0.59.
  3. Takeaway: voting amplifies an already decent call. It does not rescue a bad one. And if all five share the same flawed context, they fail together.

5.4 Split by decision boundary, not by character count

The most common decomposition mistake is to chunk text every N characters. A chunk boundary in the middle of a clause produces two pieces. Each piece lacks the context to judge it on its own. Instead, split where the decisions separate: by contract section, by ticket, by record, by paragraph. The rule: each piece must be independently judgeable. If judging piece 7 requires reading piece 6, your split is wrong or the pieces need shared context attached (a brief, a glossary, the document's definitions section prepended to each piece).

Piece sizing guidance (illustrative, tune per task): pieces of roughly 2,000–10,000 tokens each are a practical sweet spot. Below that, per-call overhead dominates. Above that, dilution and cost climb. One decision per piece. A validator between pieces.

Worked example: the 200-page contract review, with token math (illustrative prices)

Input: 200 pages, about 500 words per page, roughly 130,000 tokens. The task needs five judgments per risky clause: identify, classify risk, cite the exact language, check against policy, summarize.

Naive design: one giant call with all five instructions over 130K tokens. Result: diluted attention, no checkpoints, one uncheckable output, and the full 130K input tokens billed on every retry.

Decomposed design:

  • Split by data: 40 sections of ~3,500 tokens each (split at section boundaries, with the definitions section prepended to each piece).
  • Per section, split by task: step 1 extracts candidate clauses (cheap model), step 2 assesses risk only on candidates (strong model), step 3 formats the finding (cheap model or code).
  • Routing inside the pipeline: sections with no candidate clauses skip step 2 entirely. If 60% of sections are clean, step 2 runs 16 times instead of 40.
  • Validators: step 1 output must be valid clause references. Step 2 output must match the risk schema. The merge step dedupes overlapping findings across sections.

Token sketch: step 1, 40 calls × ~4,000 input tokens = 160K input tokens on the cheap tier. Step 2, 16 calls × ~5,000 tokens = 80K on the strong tier. Total is in the same order as the naive 130K. Every token is spent inside a focused, checkable call. Only risky sections touch the expensive model. The design also parallelizes: 40 sections run concurrently, so latency is one section's pipeline, not forty.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: a long input, a multi-part judgment, or both. Options include: one massive call with a huge context window, naive fixed-size chunking, or decision-boundary decomposition with validators and a merge step.

The trap: "use the biggest context window" (dilution, zero checkpoints) or "split into equal chunks" (boundaries cut through decisions). Chunking alone is not decomposition: real decomposition splits by decision (one judgment per piece, pieces cut at decision boundaries, validators between steps) and designs the merge with the same care as the split. The credited answer splits at decision boundaries, validates between steps, routes expensive judgment only to the pieces that need it, and defines the merge. When the scenario adds a reliability target, reach for voting and state the cost multiplier honestly.

Next: Unit 6, the four business value pillars and the SLA, the contract that turns a design into a promise.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left: the red cut lands in the middle of a clause, so each half lacks the context to judge it on its own.
  2. Right: the split follows contract sections, so each piece is independently judgeable with one decision and one validator per piece.
  3. Takeaway: if judging piece 7 requires reading piece 6, attach shared context like a brief or glossary, or your split is wrong.

Unit 6: Business value pillars and performance SLAs

Why this unit comes next.

Units 1 through 5 built the design discipline: translate the problem, architect the system, choose a pattern, orchestrate agents, decompose the work. One question remains, and the exam rewards it most: how does the business judge the result? This unit gives you the four value pillars and the SLA, the contract that turns a design into a promise.

On the board.

"The system works in the demo. Now tell me what it is worth, what you promise, and what happens when it misses". This unit turns architecture into a business case with a signed promise attached.

6.1 The four value pillars

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Every Claude solution should be able to name which pillar (or pillars) it serves. The exam lists them explicitly: efficiency (same work, fewer resources), transformation (work that was impossible before), productivity (people produce more per hour), and cost (the full economics). Underneath all four sits the performance SLA: a cheap system that misses its latency or accuracy promise destroys the value it claimed. Value claims without a measured promise are marketing. The SLA is what makes them engineering.

 EFFICIENCY      TRANSFORMATION      PRODUCTIVITY        COST
 (clock: do it   (rocket: do the     (people: amplify   (coin: the full
  faster/cheaper) previously          humans)            economics)
                 impossible)
 ============================================================
              SLA: the measured promise underneath them all
  • Efficiency: the same work, fewer resources. Tickets triaged in 30 seconds instead of 2 minutes. Documents reviewed at one-quarter the cost. Metric: unit cost or time per task, before vs after.
  • Transformation: work that was previously impossible or unaffordable. Searching 10,000 contracts for a clause pattern overnight. Personalizing onboarding for every enterprise client. Metric: new capability live, coverage achieved (e.g., "100% of contracts screened, previously 5% sampled").
  • Productivity: people produce more per hour because the system handles the grind. Drafts written, research gathered, first-pass reviews done. Metric: output per person per week, or hours returned to high-value work.
  • Cost: the full economics: build cost, run cost per unit, maintenance, and the cost of being wrong (errors, rework, incidents). Metric: total cost of ownership and unit economics (cost per ticket, per review, per query).

Performance SLAs sit underneath all four: a cheap system that misses its latency or accuracy promise destroys the value it claimed. An SLA is a promise with a measurement method and a consequence, written before launch.

How to read this diagram
  1. The four pillars: efficiency (clock: do it faster/cheaper), transformation (rocket: do the previously impossible), productivity (people: amplify humans), cost (coin: the full economics). A real project usually serves two. Name them explicitly.
  2. The foundation bar (SLAs): every pillar rests on measured promises: accuracy, latency, availability, cost ceiling. If the SLA bar cracks, the pillar above it falls: an "efficient" triage system that misroutes 30% is not efficient, it is a rework factory.
  3. The exam move: when a scenario gives you a business goal, first name the pillar, then name the SLA that guards it. "Efficiency" alone is not an answer. "efficiency guarded by a 92% routing-accuracy SLA and a 60-second p95 latency SLA" is.

6.2 SLA anatomy: what a real promise looks like

Rung 2: one level deeper. A serious SLA has five parts. Miss any of them and the promise is unenforceable:

1. METRIC       accuracy, latency, availability, cost per unit (defined precisely)
2. THRESHOLD    the number: "at least 92%", "p95 under 5 seconds" (never "fast")
3. SEGMENT      per segment, not just overall (the exam's favorite trap)
4. METHOD       how you check, how often, on what sample
5. CONSEQUENCE  what happens on a miss: rollback, page, fall back, credit
  1. The metric: accuracy, latency, availability, or cost per unit. Define it precisely: "routing accuracy" means "the fraction of tickets where the human reviewer agrees with the routing".
  2. The threshold: the number. "At least 92%." "p95 under 5 seconds." Not "fast" and not "accurate".
  3. The segment: the promise applies per segment, not just overall. This is the exam's favorite trap, straight from the blueprint's example. A contract-review assistant must hit at least 95% accuracy on EACH of five contract types. An overall 96% across 1,000 contracts can hide one type at 80%. Measure per type, fix weak types before go-live.
  4. The measurement method: how you will check, how often, on what sample. "Weekly, on 200 randomly sampled tickets, double-reviewed." A metric without a method is a rumor.
  5. The consequence: what happens on a miss. Rollback to the previous prompt version, page the owner, fall back to human review, credit the customer. The consequence is what makes teams actually watch the metric.

Two distinctions the exam tests. SLA vs SLO: the SLA is the promise to the stakeholder (with consequences). The SLO is your tighter internal target (say 94% when the SLA is 92%) that gives you warning before you breach. Model benchmarks vs system SLAs: a model's score on a public benchmark is not your system's SLA. Your system includes retrieval, tools, validators, and your data. Measure the system you ship, on your data, with your golden set.

How to read this diagram
  1. The SLA is the promise to the stakeholder, with consequences. Example: 92 percent routing accuracy.
  2. The SLO is your tighter internal target, say 94 percent. It warns you before you breach.
  3. Model benchmarks are not system SLAs. A benchmark scores the model. The SLA scores your whole system in production.
  4. What breaks: promising the SLO as the SLA. You then breach on normal variance with no tripwire left.

Latency SLAs deserve one more precision: percentiles, not averages. "p95 under 5 seconds" means 95% of requests finish within 5 seconds. Averages hide the tail. Users remember the tail. Design for the p95, and know your p99. Model latency has real variance: the same prompt can take 2 seconds or 8, depending on output length and load.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read the five cards left to right: metric, threshold, segment, method, consequence. Each card shows what the part contains and a concrete example.
  2. The red SEGMENT card is the exam's favorite trap: 96 percent overall can hide one contract type at 80 percent.
  3. Takeaway: a metric without a method is a rumor, and a threshold without a segment is a trap.

6.3 Mapping technical choices to pillars

Rung 3: the full picture. This mapping is the heart of D1's "align solutions to business value" objective. For each architectural decision, name the pillar it serves and the SLA it must not break:
Technical choice Pillar served SLA it must respect
Routing easy queries to a small model Cost, efficiency Accuracy SLA on the easy segment. Router accuracy measured separately
Parallelization (sectioning) Efficiency (latency) p95 latency SLA. Merge quality must not regress
Evaluator-optimizer loop Productivity (better drafts), transformation (higher quality bar) Accuracy SLA. Iteration cap bounds the cost SLA
Human approval gate on actions Cost (prevents expensive errors) Latency SLA gets looser by design. Say so explicitly
Multi-agent research harness Transformation (breadth impossible for one person) Accuracy SLA on synthesis. Token budget as cost ceiling
Output validation + allowlists Cost (error containment) Availability: validation must fail safe, not fail closed on everything

Notice the pattern: every row trades something. Routing trades a little accuracy risk for a lot of cost. The approval gate trades latency for safety. The exam's "most correct" answers are the ones that name the trade and pick the side the scenario's constraint demands.

How to read this diagram
  1. The amber diamond asks one question: is this action high-stakes or irreversible?
  2. The green lane auto-applies low-stakes actions and writes an audit trail.
  3. The red lane pauses high-stakes actions for human approval, then executes.
  4. What breaks: an agent that emails customers or moves money with no gate. The exam hides the missing gate.
Worked example: full ROI with the SLA attached (illustrative)

Return to the Unit 1 triage system. Build cost: 3 engineer-weeks, roughly $30,000 loaded. Run cost: 600 tickets/day × ~$0.02 = $12/day, about $3,100/year. Maintenance and weekly eval sampling: roughly $8,000/year. Year-one total: about $41,000.

Value: 9.6 human-hours saved daily at $25/hour loaded = $240/day, about $62,000/year, if the system holds 92%+ routing accuracy (the SLA). Below 92%, misroutes climb and the savings evaporate into rework: the SLA is literally what protects the ROI.

Year-one ROI: ($62,000 − $41,000) / $41,000 ≈ 0.5, or about 1.5× return. Year two (no build cost): ($62,000 − $11,000) / $11,000 ≈ 4.6×. The honest version includes the miss case. If accuracy lands at 85%, savings roughly halve and the project barely breaks even. That is why the per-segment measurement and the rollback consequence exist. An architect who presents ROI without the miss case has not finished the job.

How to read this diagram
  1. The blue bars are the costs: 3 engineer-weeks to build, the daily run cost, maintenance plus weekly eval sampling.
  2. The green bar is the value: 9.6 human-hours saved daily, about 62,000 dollars a year.
  3. The guard is the 92 percent accuracy SLA. Below it, misroutes climb and the savings evaporate into rework.
  4. What breaks: quoting ROI without the SLA. The return only exists while the accuracy promise holds.
A natural question: how do SLAs interact with model upgrades?

A model upgrade is a system change like any other: it must pass the eval loop (Unit 2) before it touches production traffic. The SLA is your contract with stakeholders, so the upgrade ships only if the golden set still passes per segment. Canary the new model on 5% of traffic, watch the SLA metrics for a week, then roll forward. Never upgrade the model and the prompt in the same change. If the SLA dips you will not know which one caused it.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: a system that "works" by one aggregate number (96% overall, average latency 3 s) with a hidden weak segment or a hidden tail. Or a business goal with a cost ceiling, where options range from the cheapest pattern to the most expensive.

Exam trap.

The trap: going live on the aggregate number, or picking the biggest model "to be safe" when a cheaper pattern meets the SLA. The blueprint's contract-review example exists to kill the sentence "our SLA is 96% accuracy". 96% overall can hide an 80% segment, and the segment is where the business risk lives.

A second trap: quoting a model vendor's benchmark as your accuracy SLA. Your system is not the vendor's benchmark. Measure your pipeline on your data. The credited answer measures per segment (and per percentile for latency), fixes weak segments before go-live, and picks the cheapest design that satisfies every stated constraint. When two options both meet the SLA, the cheaper one wins: that is the cost pillar doing its job.
