How to read this diagram
  1. Read each row left to right: the technical choice, the value pillar it serves, the SLA it must respect.
  2. Notice the pattern: every row trades something. Routing trades a little accuracy risk for a lot of cost. The approval gate trades latency for safety.
  3. Takeaway: the most correct exam answers name the trade and pick the side the scenario's constraint demands.

D1 cheat sheet and practice items

Why this section comes next.

Six units of design judgment, compressed to one page. Use this sheet to check that every pattern, guardrail, and cost rule is nameable cold before you move on.

The one-page memory

  • Translation first: pain → baseline number → decision points → narrowest pattern → test against the number. Model choice is last.
  • Four stages: input (validate, normalize, redact), processing (model + tools + state), output (validate, format, act), feedback loops (product, eval, data, human).
  • Pattern rule: known steps → workflow. Varied inputs → routing. Independent pieces → parallelization. Checkable quality → evaluator-optimizer. Big context → orchestrator-workers. Unknowable path → agent with caps and gates.
  • Multi-agent: harness over swarm. Subagents buy attention and parallelism, not fewer tokens. Cap fan-out, depth, and spend. Workers propose, orchestrator (or human) approves.
  • Decomposition: one call, one decision, one checkable output. Split at decision boundaries. Validators between steps. Always design the merge.
  • Value: name the pillar (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost). Guard it with a real SLA (metric, threshold, segment, method, consequence). Per-segment and per-percentile, never aggregate only.
  • Exam instinct: the credited answer is the narrowest design that satisfies the stated constraint. Over-engineering is the trap in roughly half the items.

The pattern selector at a glance

Can you list the steps in advance?
  YES --> Is the input varied? --YES--> ROUTING (cheap router + specialists)
   |            NO
   |             v
   |      Are pieces independent? --YES--> PARALLELIZATION
   |       |        (sectioning for speed, voting for reliability)
   |       |         NO
   |       v
   |      Is checking easier than doing? --YES--> EVALUATOR-OPTIMIZER (+ cap)
   |                    NO
   |                     v
   +---------> PROMPT CHAINING (fixed sequence + validators)
  NO ---> Is the task too big for one context? --YES--> ORCHESTRATOR-WORKERS
                       NO
                        v
              Path unknowable? --YES--> AUTONOMOUS AGENT (+ step cap, gates, logs)
                        NO --> maybe not an LLM problem: use code.

Read it top to bottom: each question eliminates a family. The surviving pattern is the narrowest one that fits the task. The guardrail in parentheses is part of the answer, not optional.

Practice items

1. A bank wants a Claude system to triage 5,000 support chats a day into 6 queues. Constraint: total model spend under $40/day, triage accuracy at least 90% per queue. Which design best fits? (A) One autonomous agent per chat that reads, decides, and replies. (B) A routing workflow: a small model classifies each chat, specialists handle each queue, low-confidence chats go to human review. (C) A single call to the largest model for every chat. (D) Fine-tune a model on last year's chats, then one call per chat.

Answer and why

B. The constraint is cost plus per-queue accuracy. Routing spends the cheap model on the easy bulk and reserves quality where it matters. The human-review lane protects the accuracy SLA on low-confidence inputs. A fails on cost and determinism (agents per chat at this volume are wildly expensive and unpredictable). C ignores the cost ceiling. D is a heavy upfront investment for a classification task a small model plus routing already solves. Fine-tuning is rarely the credited answer when a pattern satisfies the constraint.

2. A legal-tech team must review 1,000 contracts across 5 types with at least 95% accuracy on each type. Their pilot scores 96% overall, but 81% on merger agreements. The team proposes going live. As the architect, you advise: (select two) (A) Go live. 96% exceeds the target. (B) Measure per-type accuracy and hold the launch until merger agreements clear 95%. (C) Switch to a larger model and re-run the pilot. (D) Add a human-review lane for merger agreements and re-measure that segment.

Answer and why

B and D. The SLA is per segment, so the aggregate 96% is irrelevant to the merger-agreement failure. B states the correct gate. D is a legitimate architectural fix for a weak segment: route the hard segment to humans (or a stronger pipeline) and re-measure. A is the classic aggregate trap. C might help but it is a guess without diagnosis. The credited moves measure first and fix the segment deliberately.

3. A research team needs a system that investigates unfamiliar open-source projects and produces architecture summaries. Nobody can list the steps in advance: each project has a different layout, build system, and docs. Which pattern, and which guardrail is essential? (A) Prompt chaining with fixed steps. No guardrail needed. (B) Autonomous agent with tool access. Essential guardrail is a step cap plus full trace logging. (C) Routing to per-language specialists. Essential guardrail is router accuracy. (D) Evaluator-optimizer. Essential guardrail is an iteration cap.

Answer and why

B. The steps are unknowable upfront ("nobody can list the steps"), which is the textbook trigger for an agent. The essential guardrails are the step cap (unpredictable cost and runaway loops are the agent's signature risks) and full trace logging (the only way to debug a 30-step failure). A fails because fixed steps cannot cover unknown layouts. C misfires: the input variety is structural, not a clean classification problem. D needs a checkable pass criterion, which "good architecture summary" does not cleanly provide.
